sections.title: Strategic Planning Models
sections.summary: Strategic planning is the continuous, systematic process by which an organization defines what it wants to become and how it will get there. Quality managers must understand the major models — traditional three-tier planning, hoshin kanri, and scenario planning — and how mission, vision, and values guide the plan.

concepts.definition: Strategic (3–5+ years; high-level direction), Tactical (1–3 years; what tasks must be completed), and Operational (months to 1 year; day-to-day execution detailing who, what, when, how).
concepts.examTip: The exam frequently tests the distinction between strategic, tactical, and operational plans and their time horizons.

concepts.definition: A tightly knit planning and implementation system that connects management by objectives with organizational direction. Involves every level via PDCA, builds consensus through catchball, and operationalizes 'walk the talk.' Distinct from MBO — it is a complete system, not just objective-setting.
concepts.examTip: Hoshin involves EVERY level, uses PDCA, and is a whole system. Know both advantages (consensus, fact-based, alignment) and disadvantages (cultural change, 3+ years to mature, requires top-management commitment).

concepts.definition: Japanese concept used in hoshin deployment: plans are passed back and forth between levels for review and consensus before implementation, ensuring buy-in and surfacing conflicts.
concepts.examTip: Catchball ≠ delegation. It is iterative, two-way, and mandatory in hoshin.

concepts.definition: Disciplined method for imagining possible futures. In its simplest form uses three macro scenarios — good future, bad future, and wild card — to prepare contingencies and overcome tunnel vision.
concepts.examTip: Scenario planning is about preparing for uncertainty, not predicting one outcome. Three scenarios is the standard.

concepts.definition: Brief, inspiring statement of what the organization wants to become or achieve in the future. Provides direction and challenges the organization.
concepts.examTip: Vision = future state. Brief, aspirational, directional.

concepts.definition: Defines why the organization exists. Answers WHAT the organization does, WHO it serves, and HOW it delivers value.
concepts.examTip: Mission = purpose. Always answers what/who/how.

concepts.definition: Statements specifying how business is to be conducted. Customer-focused, define culture, and form the basis for ethical decision-making.
concepts.examTip: Values guide HOW; mission states WHY; vision describes WHERE.

concepts.definition: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, Time-framed, Worthwhile, Assigned, Yielding desired return. Extension of SMART used in strategic planning to ensure objectives are complete.
concepts.examTip: The exam may test any single letter. Memorize all eight.

concepts.definition: Tool that links multiyear objectives (columns) to means/initiatives (rows). Filled circle = means derived for that objective; open circle = means impacts that objective. Adds responsibility and measurement basis.
concepts.examTip: Means matrix is the bridge between goals and action plans in hoshin.

keyFigures: Mintzberg (strategy as pattern, position, and perspective)

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following BEST distinguishes hoshin kanri from traditional management by objectives?
options: Hoshin uses SMART objectives; MBO does not
Hoshin involves every level of the organization with PDCA; MBO focuses on individual objectives
MBO is a Japanese system; hoshin is American
Hoshin only applies to manufacturing; MBO applies broadly
practiceQuestions.explanation: Hoshin is a whole-organization system using PDCA loops and catchball at every level. MBO targets individual objective-setting and lacks the systemic deployment and review structure.

practiceQuestions.q: An organization plans for 3–5 years out at the corporate level. This is BEST described as:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Strategic planning operates at the 3–5+ year horizon and defines what the organization strives to become. Tactical plans (1–3 years) translate strategy into tasks; operational plans handle day-to-day execution.

practiceQuestions.q: The walkabout / catchball technique in hoshin deployment is used PRIMARILY to:
options: Calculate financial returns on each strategic objective
Surface resource conflicts and build consensus across functions
Replace formal action plans with informal agreements
Eliminate the need for senior management review
practiceQuestions.explanation: Catchball/walkabout is an iterative consensus-building mechanism that surfaces conflicts (resources, priorities, dependencies) before plans are deployed.

practiceQuestions.q: Which is NOT one of the 10 most common barriers to successful strategic planning?
options: Top management delegates the planning function to a planner
Failure to use plans as standards for measuring managerial performance
Overinvestment in planning software and tools
Top management making intuitive decisions that conflict with formal plans
practiceQuestions.explanation: Overinvestment in tools is not a recognized barrier. The other three are explicitly listed in the BoK as common strategic-planning failures.

flashcards.front: Three levels of planning and their horizons?
flashcards.back: Strategic (3–5+ yrs), Tactical (1–3 yrs), Operational (months–1 yr).

flashcards.front: What does Hoshin Kanri literally translate to?
Three macro scenarios in scenario planning?
flashcards.back: Good future, bad future, wild card.
Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, Time-framed, Worthwhile, Assigned, Yielding.
Iterative back-and-forth consensus-building between organizational levels in hoshin.
Vision = where we want to go (future state). Mission = why we exist (purpose; what/who/how).

sections.title: Business Environment Analysis
sections.summary: Senior management must continually scan internal and external environments to keep the organization viable. This includes risk analysis (SWOT, FMEA), market forces (Porter, benchmarking), stakeholder analysis, technology assessment (Quality 4.0), internal capability, and legal/regulatory factors.

concepts.definition: Systematic assessment of internal Strengths and Weaknesses and external Opportunities and Threats. Used to align strategy with reality.
concepts.formula: Internal: S, W | External: O, T
concepts.examTip: Be able to categorize items as internal (S/W) vs external (O/T). The exam tests this distinction directly.

concepts.definition: Failure Mode and Effects Analysis applied to strategic risk: identify potential failures, assess severity, occurrence, and detection, prioritize via RPN, then act.
concepts.examTip: Memorize RPN = S × O × D. All three on a 1–10 scale (10 = most severe / most frequent / lowest detection).

concepts.definition: Competitive analysis framework: existing rivalry, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers.
concepts.examTip: Know all five forces. The exam may describe a market situation and ask which force applies.

concepts.definition: Comparing organizational performance against best practices or competitors to identify improvement areas. Strategic benchmarking looks at competitive positioning, not just process metrics.
concepts.examTip: Copying competitors only makes you as good as them — benchmarking should drive innovation, not imitation.

concepts.definition: Any individual, group, or organization affected by the organization's mission. Internal: employees, shareholders, board, management, unions. External: customers, suppliers, competitors, community, government, media.
concepts.examTip: ISO 9001 uses 'interested parties' synonymously with stakeholders. Strategic objectives must align with stakeholder needs.

concepts.definition: Application of Industry 4.0 technologies to quality management: cloud computing, big data, AI/ML, IoT and edge devices, blockchain, AR/VR, mobile.
concepts.examTip: Increasingly tested. Know the four industrial revolutions and the key Quality 4.0 technologies.

concepts.definition: (1) Address behavioral changes; (2) Don't automate bad processes; (3) Solve real problems, not chase shiny objects; (4) Choose lowest tech with highest ROI; (5) Fit culture or change culture; (6) Ensure capability supports the technology.
concepts.examTip: Especially #2 — automating a bad process just speeds up bad output.

concepts.definition: Traditionalists (paper, loyal), Boomers (basic electronic), Gen X (web, independent), Millennials (on-demand, team-oriented), Gen Z (digital-native, on-demand).
concepts.examTip: Internal capability assessment must consider generational differences in learning, work style, and authority expectations.

concepts.definition: Legal: enforceable laws (employment, liability, IP, antitrust, Sarbanes-Oxley). Regulatory: rules from agencies/associations — often voluntary but with force of law.
concepts.examTip: Know the distinction. Both must inform strategic planning.

practiceQuestions.q: An FMEA shows: Severity = 8, Occurrence = 6, Detection = 5. The Risk Priority Number is:
In a SWOT analysis, 'aging facility equipment' would be classified as:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Aging equipment is an internal condition that limits performance — a Weakness. (External factors would be O or T.)

practiceQuestions.q: Porter's Five Forces does NOT include:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Government regulation is part of the broader business environment but is not one of Porter's five competitive forces.

flashcards.back: Rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power, supplier power.
Cloud, big data, AI/ML, IoT/edge, blockchain (also AR/VR, mobile).

flashcards.front: Difference between legal and regulatory factors?
flashcards.back: Legal = enforceable laws; Regulatory = agency/association rules, often voluntary but with force of law.

sections.title: Strategic Plan Deployment
sections.summary: Deployment converts plans into action: tactical plans, resource allocation, performance measurement, and quality integration. The closed-loop, cascading approach with continuous review separates plans that succeed from plans that gather dust.

concepts.definition: Project definition, completion date, link to strategic objective, scope, deliverables, measurement criteria, assumptions, approach, start date, resource estimate, capacity verification, benefit-cost estimate, Gantt timeline with responsibilities.
concepts.examTip: The exam may give a partial action plan and ask what is missing.

concepts.definition: Objectives flow from enterprise → divisional → departmental → action plans. Customer requirements feed in at each level. Borrowed from QFD.
concepts.formula: Enterprise objectives → strategies → divisional → departmental → action plans → results
concepts.examTip: Heavily tested. Cascading is the deployment mechanism — without it, plans don't reach the floor.

concepts.definition: Deployment technique: each owner posts plan on a flip chart showing required people, materials, funds. Attendees walk around, attach study notes for conflicts, then negotiate trade-offs until agreement is reached.
concepts.examTip: Walkabout = horizontal/vertical conflict surfacing tool, used before deployment locks.

concepts.definition: Performance measurement combining financial and non-financial measures. Typical perspectives: financial, customer, internal process, learning & growth.
concepts.examTip: Balanced scorecard = balance of leading and lagging indicators across multiple perspectives.

concepts.definition: 8–12 indicators selected to measure outcomes of the strategic plan. Custom-fitted to the organization. Steer the org toward fulfillment of vision/mission.
concepts.examTip: CSFs are FEW (8–12), strategic, and outcome-focused — not operational metrics.

concepts.definition: Open-loop: detect/measure inputs, rely on intuition for adjustment. Closed-loop: continuous output monitoring with immediate adjustment to action plan; produces both product/service AND control information.
concepts.examTip: Closed-loop is ALWAYS the preferred approach. Open-loop is the exam's 'wrong answer' on adjustment questions.

concepts.definition: Effectiveness = quality/correctness of the process (doing the right thing). Efficiency = speed/cost of the process (doing it well).
concepts.examTip: Effectiveness before efficiency — speeding up a wrong process is worse than slowing down a right one.

concepts.definition: Purpose (trend vs control), Cost, Rate of change, Degree of control, Consequences/risk, Baseline data availability.
concepts.examTip: These six factors determine how often to measure — exam may test any one as a scenario question.

concepts.term: Quality Policy vs Objectives vs Principles
concepts.definition: Principles: guiding beliefs. Policy: formalized document of intentions. Objectives: specific, measurable, time-bound actions to achieve quality outcomes.
concepts.examTip: Principles → Policy → Objectives is the cascade from values to measurable action.

concepts.definition: Four-step cycle: (1) Define business excellence; (2) Assess progress (e.g., Baldrige); (3) Identify gaps vs world-class; (4) Deploy action plan with annual priorities and aligned metrics.
concepts.examTip: This is hoshin's annual review mechanism — connects strategic plan with continual improvement.

practiceQuestions.q: A closed-loop operation is preferred over an open-loop because it:
options: Provides continuous monitoring and immediate adjustment
Reduces the cost of all measurement equipment
practiceQuestions.explanation: Closed-loop produces two outputs — the product/service AND the information needed to manage and improve the process. Open-loop relies on intuition for adjustment.

practiceQuestions.q: Critical Success Factors should typically number:
practiceQuestions.explanation: 8–12 CSFs is the recognized range — enough to span strategic goals without diluting focus.

practiceQuestions.q: The cascading concept in deployment originates from which quality methodology?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Cascading borrows from QFD's House-of-Quality logic of translating customer requirements through successive matrices.

flashcards.back: Enterprise → Divisional → Departmental → Action plans → Results, with customer requirements feeding in.
Posting plans on flip charts, walking around, attaching conflict notes, then resolving trade-offs.

flashcards.front: Open vs closed loop — which is preferred?

flashcards.back: Effectiveness = doing the right thing. Efficiency = doing it well/fast/cheap.
